Chinese humanoid robots broke records set by humans, including Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record, on the opening day of the Olympics-like World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday. More than 2,000 humanoid robots were participating in the event, organisers said. In a 100-metre sprint, a humanoid robot achieved a result of 9.39 seconds, beating the human record of 9.58 seconds set by Jamaican athlete Bolt in 2009. In a standing high jump, a humanoid robot was able to reach 2.88m, well above the 0.95m best result by a humanoid in last year’s first edition of the games. It surpassed the human high jump record of 2.45m set by Cuba’s Javier Sotomayor in 1993. The five-day games, now in their second year, are a spectacle demonstrating China’s rapid progress in advanced robotics as the technology race with the US heats up. There are 51 events and more than 1,000 competitions taking place, including running, table tennis and football. For more news, visit @sbsnews_au (link in bio).

artist and automata maker Amedeo Capelli, known as Stoccafisso Design, creates playful mechanical sculptures from wood, wire and simple mechanisms. In his recent shrimp automata, a handmade crustacean comes to life through a system of wooden gears, cams, rods and rotating parts hidden beneath the stage. Turning the crank transfers motion through the mechanism, making the shrimp’s body and limbs move in an exaggerated, almost theatrical way. Capelli’s work combines traditional automata-making, kinetic sculpture and humor. Instead of hiding the mechanics, he often leaves them visible, allowing us to understand how a simple rotation can be transformed into surprisingly complex movement. #shrimp #art #artist #niche #weird

I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

✨REMEMBER TO SHARE THIS✨ In 2016, the Guggenheim Museum commissioned its very first robotic artwork called Can’t Help Myself (Wannmann, 2016). The artwork is created by two of China’s artists Sun Yuan and Peng Yu and can be described as a robotic arm that has one specific, life-long duty: to prevent the deep-red, bloodlike liquid, which constantly oozes outwards, from straying too far. By dragging its sweeper across the floor in calculated, almost dance-like movements, the robot brings the liquid back into place over and over again, without it ever seeming to stop. In an effort to clean up the constant mess, the robot only makes matters worse by leaving smudges of the liquid on the floor, the walls, and itself. In the video , you can see the robot in action. This led to the robot slowing down enormously and eventually being unplugged in 2019. Apr 12, 2026 You won’t believe your eyes, a real humanoid robot is out on the streets at night, running full speed and successfully herding a group of wild boars straight back into the forest. This is Edward Warchocki, a compact Unitree G1 humanoid robot standing about 132 cm tall. In this incredible clip, he charges behind a pack of “dziki”,  the wild boars that have become a serious urban problem across Poland. The animals scatter and bolt as the robot stays right on their heels, guiding them away from houses, gardens, and roads until they disappear into the treeline. Why is this happening? Wild boars have exploded in numbers in Polish towns and suburbs. With no natural predators left and plenty of easy food from trash bins, compost, and backyard gardens, they wander into residential areas every night. They root up lawns, damage property, knock over fences, and can become aggressive when surprised, creating real safety risks for families, pets, and drivers. Traditional solutions like hunting or fencing often fall short in crowded neighborhoods. That’s where Edward comes in. Instead of sending humans into potentially dangerous nighttime encounters, this innovative team is testing a non-lethal, high-tech solution: a fast, fearless robot that can patrol and scare the boars away safely and effectively. The footage shows it working perfectly,  the robot’s movement, lights, and presence are enough to make the boars turn tail and head back to the woods where they belong. This isn’t a movie scene or special effects. It’s actual, real world footage from a Polish town where wild boar invasions are a daily headache. Edward Warchocki, already famous for public appearances and his quirky personality, is now proving robots can handle practical problems in creative new ways. From dodging traffic to chasing boars, the future of everyday robotics is here, and it’s happening right now in Poland. Absolutely wild, totally real, and surprisingly effective.  Wild boars thought they owned the streets at night… until Edward showed up for his evening workout .
